answer.why: As an insider, that title made me laugh straight away. Confirmed and substantive is exactly the wording on the letter you wait years for, so it feels like someone who has actually sat through appraisal cycles wrote it. Minister Salary is the obvious hook and would get more taps from the general public, but it reads like clickbait or a political jab, and I'd half expect it to get the details wrong. I would still tap Minister Salary out of curiosity if the other one weren't there.
answer.expect_minister_salary: A cheeky, headline-grabbing sim about the pay-benchmark debate, probably with a lot of smirking about how much ministers earn and a power-fantasy climb to the top. I'd expect a broad, slightly satirical take with outsider details and the odd wrong title or grade, and I'd worry it would turn into a pay-packet clicker rather than a career game.
answer.expect_confirmed_substantive: A drier, more insider game about the slow grind of the service: probation, confirmation, acting appointments versus substantive ones, waiting on ranking exercises and appraisal wording. I'd expect dry humour about process, small career-defining moments, and a quieter, more authentic feel. Maybe a bit niche, and the name might mean nothing to outsiders, but it signals the makers know the system.

best_moment.what: Y21 in my notes: the Officer You Nominated came back. I nominated a quiet officer for PSLP at Y10, she rose to Deputy Secretary, and I let her decide without lobbying. It felt like how the service actually works, quietly, over years.

worst_moment.what: Losing the ward at 48.2% right after I chose to campaign on the record. The card said it was never about me, so the choices felt irrelevant, and it ended abruptly.

The ending's EXPOSURE line said my file was clean enough to be boring

answer.held_back_by: Honestly, a mix of principled choices that cost STAND with the party and a ceiling the game set quietly at the start. I answered things straight and the party rewarded that less than the service does, and the final loss was down to the ward, not me.
answer.ending_fair_why: Fair in tone: losing a GRC-type contest at 48.2% is realistic and the card said it was not about me. But I was a bit annoyed that the vote result barely seemed tied to my choices, and I was never shown it coming.
answer.chase_next: The Deputy Prime Minister ending, since the card says my Y21 choice raised the ceiling to that. I would want to see what else raises STAND, and I would try to understand what the party actually rewards.
answer.play_again_why: I enjoyed the institutional detail, but I have just seen the whole arc and want to let it sit. I might replay if a friend told me STAND can be managed without giving up integrity.

tone_breaks.line: Y4: a director said 'this system is a joke'
tone_breaks.note: This read as the game commenting on itself, a wink at the player rather than a plausible thing for a director to say in front of a junior.

tone_breaks.line: When you joined, your file estimated your potential at Director. You were not told.
tone_breaks.note: Close to real, since potential is estimated, but the officer is never told the number, and the blunt 'Director' label sounds off. The estimate would be a band tied to the scheme, not a single title.

answer.title_fit_why: The game is really about slow, quiet progress through grades, appraisal wording and trust, not a salary chase. 'Minister Salary' makes it sound like the point is the money and the cynicism.

Lost the Ward

Forty-eight point two percent. You shook every hand in that ward and it was not enough, and it was never going to be about you anyway.

LIFETIME EARNINGS $9.22M
INTEGRITY 100

YOUR CEILING: When you joined, your file estimated your potential at Director. You were not told.
